text: Learning which objects may safely contact each other.
Operate high-risk manual kitchen tools (e.g., mandoline slicer, box grater) without damaging the tool or the robot's end-effectors.
Skim foam or fat off the top of a boiling liquid.
Clean out and replace an aquarium or terrarium filter.

Wake someone up; help someone sit, stand, or steady themselves; offer an arm on stairs; help with buttons, zips, and shoes; fetch and clean glasses and hearing aids; push or fold a wheelchair or walker.
Sick-day care: take a temperature, bring fluids, tissues, and a heating pad, clean up after vomiting, fetch an inhaler or EpiPen, bring medication on the person's own schedule and log it.

Primitives: communication is thin (you have Report, Alert, and Ask for clarification). Add Speak, Listen, Announce, Explain, Confirm, Refuse, Undo, Hand off to a human, Remember, Forget. Physical verbs also missing: Cut/Slice, Peel, Crack, Tear, Hammer, Drill, Climb, Kneel/Crouch, Balance, Throw/Catch, Point/Gesture, Spray, Brush.

section: Reaching, climbing, and fixing. Tool handling stops at basic hand tools, and there's no height access.
text: Repairs: paint walls and touch up scuffs, caulk a tub or sink, patch small holes, sand, regrout, pressure-wash, seal a deck.
Clean up broken glass and ceramic, spilled flour, sugar, or oil, vomit, urine, and pet accidents.
Pests: remove insects and spiders, clean ant trails, set and check traps, report droppings or nests, empty standing water, pantry-moth and fruit-fly traps.
Maintain other household robots: empty the robot vacuum, clean its brushes, refill the mop tank, rescue it when stuck, clear cords and socks before it runs.

Pets beyond feeding and walking. Give owner-directed medication, bathe and dry a dog, check for ticks and fleas, open and close crates, keep pets' meals separate, calm a pet during storms or fireworks. Aquarium water changes, filter, and glass, small-animal cages, and backyard chickens (eggs, coop, water) are also missing.
Food safety: avoid cross-contamination (raw-meat boards, hands), control allergens (read labels, clean shared tools), discard food left out too long.
“Make this place look nice.” There may be no single correct state; it has to reason about symmetry, spacing, aesthetics, furniture placement, and household preferences.
“Get this out of here.” It must determine whether that means trash it, relocate it, store it, return it, or simply move it to another room.
“Make this usable again.” Could mean clearing clutter, reconnecting something, cleaning it, reorganizing it, or finding missing components.
“Set this room up for a party.” Number of guests, seating, food locations, walking paths, decorations, trash locations, and breakable objects all matter.
“Do the important stuff first.” Requires ranking chores by urgency and impact.
“Grab something I can use as a bowl.” Requires functional substitution rather than object-label matching.
“Find something waterproof to put under this.” Requires material-property reasoning.
“Move everything off this table except what we still need.” Requires understanding the current activity.
“Don’t disturb my setup.” It has to understand which relationships between objects must remain unchanged.
“Find where that smell is coming from.” Requires active investigation across rooms and possible causes.
“Figure out why the floor is wet.” Could be spilled water, a leak, pet water, rain, appliance overflow, etc.
“Something fell upstairs. Check what happened.” Requires investigating an uncertain event.
“Wash these without ruining anything.” Requires reading tags, recognizing fabric, colors, special treatments, and machine capabilities.
“Get this stain out.” Requires identifying probable stain/material combination and choosing an appropriate treatment.
“Make these shoes look better.” Different materials require different cleaning methods.
“Prepare the backyard for people.” Requires inspecting and deciding what matters: seating, debris, shade, toys, wet surfaces, pet waste, etc.
“Clean up after the storm.” Requires adapting to unpredictable debris and possibly unsafe conditions.
“Keep the cat out while you clean this room.” Requires simultaneous task execution and dynamic agent management.
“Don’t make it worse.” Requires uncertainty-aware behavior and conservative intervention.
“Do it without moving the sleeping baby.” Requires low-noise, low-vibration planning.
“Do it without waking anyone up.” Requires reasoning about doors, floors, lights, vacuum noise, dishes, etc.
“Wait until I’m done with that.” Requires recognizing task dependencies.
“Finish this after they leave.” Requires postponed task memory.
“Do this before it becomes a problem.” Requires predictive maintenance reasoning.
“Don’t throw away anything important.” Requires high precision and conservative uncertainty handling.
“Throw away anything obviously useless.” Requires semantic and personal-value judgment.
“Clean the inside of this computer.” The robot must distinguish between dust and delicate capacitors, knowing how much physical force (or air pressure) is safe to apply near a motherboard.
“Read the room.” If humans are having a tense argument, or someone is crying, the robot must infer that it should cancel its noisy vacuuming task and leave quietly.
“The toilet’s overflowing — do something!” Requires improvising a response (shutoff valve, float, towels) with no named procedure.
“Is it dry yet?” (laundry, paint, a mopped floor) Requires judging state from sparse cues.
“Don’t buy anything; use what we have.” Requires substitution under resource limits.
